title: Understanding Stationarity
text: Stationarity is an important concept within time series analysis. Some types of statistical time series models such as ARIMA require a time series to be stationary.

title: Understanding Stationarity
text:
Defining Stationarity
In simple terms, stationarity describes how stable a time series is, specifically with regards to the mean and variance of the time series.
A stationary time series is one with a relatively stable mean and variance. This does not mean the time series is completely flat, with no fluctuations; it just means that, over the course of time, the mean and variance of the data are relatively stable. A non-stationary time series is one which has a mean or variance that are not consistent over time.

title: Understanding Stationarity
section: Determining whether a Time Series is Stationary
text:
Determining whether a Time Series is Stationary
There are two main ways to identify whether a time series is stationary or non-stationary: visualization and statistical tests. We will explore each of these briefly.

Visualization
If a time series has a trend or seasonality, it is non-stationary. Understanding the structure of your time series, then, can be a quick way to determine whether or not your time series is stationary. The easiest way to do this is by visualizing your time series. Often a simple line plot can reveal trend or seasonality, or you can decompose your time series. See this article for more information about time series structures and decomposition.
Let’s first take a look at an example of a non-stationary time series.



electricity production line plot


This line graph displays the monthly electricity production from 1985-2018. Just a cursory glance indicates that neither the mean nor the variance are consistent over time. There is a clear upward trend to the data as well as increasing seasonal variance as well. This gives us strong evidence that we are dealing with a non-stationary data set.
Now, let’s see an example of a stationary time series.



google stock price change 2010


This line graph displays the daily change in the opening stock price for Google’s stock in 2010. What we see here is that, while there are certainly day-to-day fluctuations, the overall mean and variance appear to be relatively stable. There does not appear to be a trend to the data or consistent seasonal fluctuations.


Statistical Tests
At times, the visual evidence may be unclear, particularly if you have a noisy data set. In this case, you should use a statistical test to check whether your time series is stationary or non-stationary. There are different statistical tests available, but the most common is called the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test.
This test checks the time series for the presence of something called a “unit root”. If there is a unit root present, it indicates a non-stationary time series. The test operates with the following hypotheses:

Null Hypothesis: Has Unit Root (Time Series is Non-Stationary)
Alternate Hypothesis: Does not Have Unit Root (Time Series is Stationary)

A p-value of below .05 is typically interpreted as strong evidence to reject the null hypothesis, while a p-value of above .05 is interpreted as insufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. In other words, a p-value below .05 is interpretted as evidence for a stationary time series; a p-value above .05 is interpretted as evidence of a non-stationary time series. Note, this test, though helpful, is not a 100% guarantee. It should always be paired with visual exploration prior to model creation and additional testing of the model’s performance.
The statsmodels adfuller function performs this test for us. Let’s run our electricity production data from earlier in the article through the adfuller test as an example.

import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

elec_production = pd.read_csv('Electric_Production.csv')
elec_production['DATE'] = pd.to_datetime(elec_production['DATE'])
elec_production = elec_production.rename(columns={'DATE': 'date', 'IPG2211A2N': 'electricity_production'})
elec_production = elec_production.set_index('date')
elec_production = elec_production.asfreq('MS')

elec_adf_result = adfuller(elec_production)
print('adf p-value:', elec_adf_result[1])

adf p-value: 0.18621469116586592


The p-value in our adfuller results is greater than the critical value of .05. This gives us additional evidence that we are dealing with a non-stationary time series, confirming what we observed from the visualization. If our p-value was below .05, that would typically be interpretted as evidence that of stationarity in our data.
In future articles, we will explore this idea of stationarity further. We will consider additional examples and look at how we can make a non-stationary time series stationary by differencing the data set.
To explore the topic of differencing your data, visit our article here.

title: Time Series Structures
text: This articles explores the main structural elements to look for when exploring a time series data set and gives a basic example of time series decomposition.

title: Time Series Structures
text:
Time Series Structures
There are four main structures to look for when you are exploring a time series data set. Understanding these structural elements is an important part of learning about your time series, determining which preprocessing steps are needed, and deciding which models would be most appropriate for forecasting.

Trend
A trend is a long-term increase or decrease in the data. It describes an overall direction of the data set, whether upward or downward.
The following line plot of the daily Google opening stock price from 2004 to 2022 illustrates a clear example of an upward trend. If, on the other hand, the overall direction of the data appeared to be “flat”, this would likely indicate the absence of a trend.



Google stock price line chart




Seasonality
Seasonality describes repeating fluctuations that occur at consistent intervals. These could show up as “peaks” or “valleys” in your time series data. For example, if you are a marketing analyst for a large online toy retailer, you might see regular, recurring spikes in sales in Q4 of each year around the holidays. This is a form of seasonality. Depending on the granularity of your data set, it could occur at other frequencies such as on certain days of the week or during certain hours of the day. The key is that it is of a consistent and repeating pattern.
The following plot of monthly electricity production from 2009-2018 shows clear seasonal structure. This seasonality aligns with what we intuitively would expect about electricity use. The highest electricity production is in the winter and, to a lesser extent, in the summer. Spring and fall show relatively lower levels of production. This pattern is repeating and at consistent intervals. If, on the other hand, the fluctuations in the data appeared to be random, with no clear pattern, we would not consider them to be seasonal in nature.



Electricity production line chart




Cycles
Cycles describe longer term rises and falls in a data set that do repeat but not at a consistent interval. These are very commonly discussed in the field of economics and finance. Unlike seasonality, cycles are often difficult to predict.
The following plot of solar activity from 1909-2009 shows a clear cyclical pattern in the data. The increases and decreases in solar activity are longer in nature than seasonal fluctuations and are more difficult to anticipate.



Solar activity line chart




Noise
Whatever is left over after accounting for the time series structures described so far is the noise in the data set. Noise consists of random fluctuations in the data that cannot be attributed to any perceivable structure. A time series data set that has no perceivable structure is called “white noise”. In the real world, virtually all time series data will have some amount of noise in it.

title: Time Series Structures
text:
Time Series Decomposition
Time series decomposition is the process of taking a time series data set and splitting it apart into its different structures. Using the flights data set from the seaborn package in Python, let’s walk through a simple example of time series decomposition. To accomplish this, we’ll rely on statsmodels’ seasonal_decompose function.
Note, the model parameter is very important. If seasonality remains at a consistent level, you can use “additive”. If the seasonal fluctuations become more extreme as the time series increases, you will want to use “multiplicative”. We will explore this further in another article. For more information check out the statsmodels documentation here: https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.seasonal_decompose.html
For more complex time series or time series with extreme outliers, you should consider using STL decomposition. More information is available here: https://www.statsmodels.org/devel/generated/statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL.html

#Necessary imports
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose

#Load flights data into 'flights' dataframe
flights = sns.load_dataset("flights")

#You will often need to convert your data into a more usable form, usually with some type of time index.
#This code converts the 'year' and 'month' columns into a single datatime column then sets that column as our index.

flights['date'] = pd.to_datetime(
    flights['year'].astype(str) + '-' + flights['month'].astype(str), format='%Y-%b'
)

flights = flights.set_index('date')

#Separate the target feature into a series. We no longer need the month/year columns since our index  already has that information.
y = flights['passengers']

#Use the seasonal_decompose function to decompose your time series, be sure to choose the correct model parameter
flights_decomp = seasonal_decompose(
                    y,
                    #model='additive',
                    model='multiplicative'
                )
fig = flights_decomp.plot()
fig.set_size_inches(8, 6);








The resulting plots give us the decomposed version of the time series. This can be extremely helpful in understanding the structure of our data.
The first line graph is the original data set without any decomposition.
The second reveals the trend in the data.
The third reveals the seasonality in the data.
The final plot reveals the residuals (or noise) in the data set. For additive, this should cluster around 0. For multiplicative, this should cluster around 1. You hope to not see remaining structure or changing variance in the residuals.
In the case of the flights data set, we can clearly see a consistent upward trend. We also see strong seasonal fluctuations, with spikes and valleys occurring at consistent points each year. Finally, we see that the residuals appear to have little to no remaining structure and are tightly clustered around 1.
Often times, your data sets may not decompose this cleanly. However, this is an important exercise that is very helpful in learning about the underlying time series structures.

title: Time Series Structures
text:
Conclusion
To sum up, the four main structures you are looking for within your time series are trend, seasonal fluctuations, cycles, and noise. Time series decomposition can be a useful tool in exploring these aspects of your time series.

title: Naive Forecasts with Trend
text:
In past articles, we have covered simple naive forecasting and seasonal naive forecasting. The final type of naive forecasting method we will cover is a naive forecast with drift. This allows us to account for trend in our time series.
This article will first explore the key concepts behind a naive forecast with drift. We will then walk through a simple example demonstrating how to build this type of forecast in Python.

title: Naive Forecasts with Trend
section: Why a Simple Naive Forecast is Often Not Enough
text:
Why a Simple Naive Forecast is Often Not Enough
As a reminder, a simple naive forecast model uses the most recent past value in your time series as the next predicted value. In other words, the value at t becomes the forecast for t+1. One limitation of this method is that it does not capture any trend in your time series.
A trend is a long-term increase or decrease in your time series. For more information about trend and other time series structures, check out this article. If your data is increasing or decreasing over time, that will not be accounted for in a simple naive forecast.
If you are only forecasting one or two steps into the future, this may not be a big problem. However, the stronger the trend and the further in the future you want to forecast out, the more your simple naive forecast will deviate from the actual results.

title: Naive Forecasts with Trend
text:
How To Calculate Drift
The term “drift” refers to the constant increment we add to our forecast to account for an estimated trend. There are different ways to calculate this value.
One approach is to simply find the difference between your two most recent observations. This method has the advantage of capturing the most recent change in your time series. However, if the last two observations are not representative of the underlying trend in your data, this may not be a good way to estimate future changes.
Another approach is to find the difference between the first and last observations in your dataset and divide this value by the total number of observations minus one. This gives us the average change across our time series.
This is the conventional approach used in a naive forecast with drift. Its advantage is that it captures the average change across the entire time series rather than relying on just the most recent observations. However, if the trend has changed recently, it may not fully capture that change in future forecasts.

title: Naive Forecasts with Trend
section: How to Include Drift in a Naive Forecast
text:
How to Include Drift in a Naive Forecast
Regardless of how you calculate the drift value, the way you incorporate it into your forecast is the same.
Without seasonality, your forecast for the next time step becomes the previous observed value plus the drift value. As you move further into the future, you continue adding the drift value at each successive step.
This allows the drift to accumulate over time, which is what makes this method capable of approximating a trend into the future.
If you are adding drift to a seasonal naive forecast, the calculation requires accounting for both the seasonal pattern and the accumulated drift. We will provide an example of this in a future article. For now, however, we will focus on a naive forecast with drift that does not include seasonality.

title: Naive Forecasts with Trend
text:
A Simple Example in Python
To illustrate a naive forecast with drift, we will use a common time series dataset that captures three years of monthly shampoo sales. In the following code cell, we will load the libraries we need and prepare our data for use.

# common imports
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# load the shampoo sales time series dataset
shampoo = pd.read_csv('shampoo_sales.csv')

# The following code creates the datetime index. 
# We are not told the exact years this data was collected from, so 1995-1997 will be used.

shampoo['Year'] = pd.Series([
    1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 1995, 
    1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996, 1996,
    1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997, 1997
])
shampoo['Date'] = shampoo['Year'].astype('str') + '-' + shampoo['Month'].str[-2:] + '-01'
shampoo['Date'] = pd.to_datetime(shampoo['Date'])
shampoo = shampoo.set_index('Date')
shampoo.index.freq = 'MS'
shampoo = shampoo.drop(columns=['Month', 'Year'])

Now, we will perform a simple train-test split to set aside a portion of our dataset for testing.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

y_train, y_test = train_test_split(shampoo, shuffle=False, test_size=4) #Shuffle parameter is set to Fase since we are working with a time series

Let’s take a quick look at our data using a simple line plot. In a real-world project, you would do much more during the exploratory data analysis stage. However, for our purposes, this will help us identify the trend structure within the data.

shampoo.plot(figsize=(10,7))
plt.title('Shampoo Sales by Month: 1995-1997')
plt.ylabel('Units Sold')
plt.show();








There is no clear seasonality in this dataset. However, our data displays a strong upward trend. Shampoo sales steadily increased during the years the data was collected.
Now we are ready to create our fitted values for the training set. We will use pandas’ .shift() method to shift our values forward by one row. Then, we will use the .dropna() method to remove the resulting null value created by this shift.

shampoo_naive_fitted = y_train.shift(1)
shampoo_naive_fitted = shampoo_naive_fitted.dropna()

Next, we calculate our drift value. In this example, we will calculate it by subtracting the first observation from the last observation in our training set and dividing by the number of observations minus one.
Pandas’ .squeeze() method turns the resulting single-value Series into a scalar value. More information about this method can be found in the pandas documentation here.

shampoo_naive_drift = ((y_train.iloc[-1] - y_train.iloc[0]) / (len(y_train) - 1)).squeeze()

print(shampoo_naive_drift)

4.5677419354838715


Our drift value is approximately 4.6. This means that, on average, our data has increased by around 4.6 units of sales each month across the training period.
We will now add this drift value to our fitted values to create a naive forecast with drift.

# Add drift to fitted values
shampoo_naive_fitted_drift = shampoo_naive_fitted + shampoo_naive_drift

#Rename columns to make future visualization easier
shampoo_naive_fitted_drift = shampoo_naive_fitted_drift.rename(columns={'Sales': 'naive_forecast'})

Okay, now we are ready to forecast into our test period. We will add the drift value at each successive step, allowing it to accumulate as we move further into the future.
We will start with the last actual observation in our training set and calculate the forecast for each step in the test period.

# Capture the final actual training observation as our starting point
last_observation = y_train.iloc[-1].squeeze()

# Create a forecast extending through the test period
shampoo_naive_forecast_drift = pd.DataFrame(
    index=y_test.index
)

# Create a step column to track the forecast horizon
shampoo_naive_forecast_drift['step'] = np.arange(
    1, len(y_test) + 1
)

# Calculate the forecast by adding the accumulated drift
shampoo_naive_forecast_drift['naive_forecast'] = (
    last_observation +
    shampoo_naive_forecast_drift['step'] * shampoo_naive_drift
)

# Drop the step column since it is no longer needed
shampoo_naive_forecast_drift = shampoo_naive_forecast_drift.drop(
    columns=['step']
)

Ok, we have successfully projected our naive model with drift through the test period. Let’s now take a moment to examine how well our model performs using a simple visualization.

pd.concat([shampoo, pd.concat([shampoo_naive_fitted_drift, shampoo_naive_forecast_drift], axis=0)], axis=1).rename(columns={'Sales':'actual'}).plot(figsize=(10, 7))
plt.axvline(x=y_train.index[-1], color='red', linestyle='--', label='Start of Test Set')
plt.title('Shampoo Sales by Month: Naive with Trend Forecast vs. Actuals')
plt.ylabel('Units Sold')
plt.legend()
plt.show();








Based on this visualization, our naive model with drift did a good job of capturing the upward trend in our time series as it extended into the test period.
A simple naive model, by comparison, would have produced a flat forecast line and increasingly underpredicted shampoo sales.
We should keep in mind that this is a small dataset, and the test set in particular is very small. Our model may not perform as well as it extends further into the future.

title: Naive Forecasts with Trend
text:
Conclusion
To sum up, by calculating a drift term and adding it at each successive step of a simple naive forecast, we can approximate a trend in our time series. This can be accomplished fairly easily in Python.
This type of model is easy to understand and not computationally intensive. While it may be suitable as a production model in certain situations, it is more commonly used as a baseline model against which we can compare more advanced forecasting methods.
One important limitation to remember is that a naive forecast with drift assumes the average rate of change will remain relatively consistent into the future. If the underlying trend changes, the model may not perform as well.
In a future article, we will look at how to combine both seasonality and trend in the same naive forecast.

title: Intro to Time Series
text: In this article, we will cover the basics of time series data - what it is, why it matters, and how it is unique.

title: Intro to Time Series
text:
What is a Time Series?
A time series is a data set in which the observations, the instances, or the rows, are in some type of sequential order. Consider the following example from a data set that includes average march temperatures for the state of Pennsylvania from 1895-2026:

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

pa_march_temps = pd.read_csv('pa_avg_temp_march_1895_2026.csv')
pa_march_temps['Year'] = pa_march_temps['Date'].astype(str).str[0:4].astype(int)
pa_march_temps = pa_march_temps.drop(['Date'], axis=1).copy()
pa_march_temps = pa_march_temps.set_index('Year')
pa_march_temps = pa_march_temps.rename(columns={'Value': 'March Avg Temp - Degrees F'})
pa_march_temps.head(10)

Notice that the index for our data set is in years, and these years are in sequential (generally, chronological) order. This is what makes it a time series.
Time series are arranged along a timeline. There is a chronological order to the data, and typically the index is temporal in nature. Interestingly, other types of data follow similar patterns to time series without being temporal in nature. DNA sequencing, noise, and sound frequencies, for example, can follow many of the same patterns that time series do, and many of the same rules apply. We will not delve into those applications here, but it is good to know that they exist.
The main point is that, when it comes to time series data, order matters. There is a sequence to the rows, to the instances, and to the observations.

title: Intro to Time Series
text:
Regular and Irregular Time Series
Time series data can fit into two categories: regular time series and irregular time series. This refers to the frequency of the data. Most of the data you will work with are regular time series, meaning the observations occur at a consistent frequency. Daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, and yearly data are all examples of regular time series.
Irregular time series, unlike regular time series, do not have consistent spacing. Consider a machine that records a timestamp, along with information about what happened, every time it malfunctions or produces an error. The spacing between those records is random, which produces an irregular time series. This is just one example. Regular time series are much easier to work with, so an irregular time series is often converted into a regular time series through a process called resampling, which we will cover in a future article.

title: Intro to Time Series
section: The Prevalance of Time Series Data
text:
The Prevalance of Time Series Data
Time series are important regardless of the industry or field in which you work. Time affects everything around us; everything that happens in our world takes place in time. There are countless, almost infinite, examples. Here are just a few:

Weather conditions, such as the daily average temperature or monthly rainfall
Stock market data, such as the daily closing prices of stocks
Medical data, such as a patient’s heart rate taken every second
Transportation data, such as the monthly number of flight passengers in the US
Economic data, such as the annual GDP of the United States
Wildlife data, such as the number of wolf sightings each month in Yellowstone National Park
Sales and marketing data, such as quarterly sales of a certain product
Law enforcement data, such crime statistics in Louisville, KY for the past 10 years

The list could go on. Time series are literally everywhere. Can you think of an example of time series data in your company or organization?
If you are a data professional, sooner or later you will work with time series. This is why it is so crucial to learn how to understand and handle time series data.

title: Intro to Time Series
text:
How are Time Series Unique?
You may be asking why we need separate training and instruction for working with time series data. “Could I not apply the same methods, concepts, and models that I learned on other types of data to time series?” The answer is: “not exactly”. Many of the same ideas and steps carry over, but there are also many differences. The following are the key differences that make working with time series unique. We will expand upon these in much greater detail in future articles.

Key Difference #1: Order Matters
The first key difference with time series is that the order of the data is important. The index of a time series provides a sequential order for the observations. We cannot shuffle a time series the way we would shuffle a cross-sectional data set, because shuffling destroys many of the things that make the time series valuable, including the ways we can use it to predict future values. For this reason, order matters.


Key Difference #2: Autocorrelation
The second key difference is autocorrelation. This is a fancy word that simply means correlation with itself. The data in a time series are typically not independent of each other; one instance may depend heavily on the instance that came before it. Think of a time series like setting up a line of dominos next to each other. If you push the first domino, each successive domino is impacted. This is a simple illustration for how instances of a time series impact future instances. There is a great deal of correlation within many time series, and models are often built by using that autocorrelation to your advantage. We are therefore not dealing with independent instances, as we often want to with other types of data.


Key Difference #3: Structure
Time series have unique structures that are extremely informative for understanding the series and for predicting its future instances. Examples of time series structural elements include trends, seasonality, and cycles. This is one reason we rely heavily on visualization. Visualization is always important when working with data, but with time series data it is irreplaceable. You have to be able to visualize your data in order to grasp the underlying structure.


Key Difference #4: Unique Preparation and Models
Because of the points above, there are unique preparation steps to take when planning and choosing a model. Examples include rolling-horizon cross-validation, which we will cover in the future; not shuffling your data set, as already mentioned; and ensuring that you have a datetime index to work from. At times you may need to perform a process called differencing on your data set. We will cover these preparation steps in more detail later. There are also models designed specifically for time series, such as ARIMA, exponential smoothing, and state space models, as well as variations of models you may have used with cross-sectional data but designed with time series in mind.


Key Difference #5: Different Goals
With time series, we are often, though not always, trying to predict outside the range of known values; we are predicting the future. With other data sets, the goal is often to predict within the bounds of the sample data. Time series are different, and we often approach them with the specific goal of forecasting in mind.

title: Intro to Time Series
text:
Conclusion
To sum it up: because time series are all around us and unique, we as data professionals must equip ourselves to work with them effectively.

title: Additive vs. Multiplicative Seasonality
text:
Seasonal patterns are one of the key structures we look for when analyzing time series data sets.
Seasonality refers to repeating patterns in a time series that occur at consistent intervals. For example, a drive-through coffee shop consistently sees their peak customer traffic around 7:30am Monday-Friday. This would be a form of seasonality.
However, not all seasonality is the same. There are two main types of seasonal fluctuations that a time series may possess. These are additive or multiplicative seasonality. Being able to identify which type of seasonality you are working with is important if you plan to use time series decomposition or model your time series data.
In the rest of this article, we will explain what each of these types of seasonality are, then we will walk through how to use visualizations in Python to identify each.

title: Additive vs. Multiplicative Seasonality
text:
Additive Seasonality
A time series has additive seasonality if the seasonal fluctuations are consistent in size, regardless of whether the underlying data increases or decreases.
Let’s return to our coffee shop scenario from earlier in this article. Let’s say the coffee shop just opened for business a month ago and gets around 7 customers each half hour interval on average. The peak customer traffic occurs from 7:30am-8:00am on weekdays and the shop typically has 5 additional customers over the 7 customer average during that morning interval.
Now, let’s imagine that the coffee shop gets very popular over its first year of business. A year later, the coffee shop now gets around 12 customers each half hour interval on average. Additive seasonality in this case would mean that the 7:30am-8:00am interval would still get 5 additional customers over that average level.
In other words, the seasonal variation stays consistent - even though the underlying trend has caused the overall customer traffic at the coffee shop to increase.

title: Additive vs. Multiplicative Seasonality
text:
Multiplicative Seasonality
A time series has multiplicative seasonality if the seasonal fluctuations change in size as the underlying data increases or decreases.
Let’s return to our coffee shop illustration once more. Imagine that a month in, the increased customer traffic was 5 over the average from 7:30am-8:00am. So far, exactly the same as our prior scenario. This time though, imagine that a year later, as the average customer traffic increased, the variation during that 7:30am interval also increased to 2 times as many customers than the average (+12 customers). This would be an example of multiplicative seasonality. As overall customer counts increased, the seasonal variation in our peak interval also increased.
In other words, the seasonal variation increases or decreases based on the underlying trend.

title: Additive vs. Multiplicative Seasonality
section: Using Visualization to Determine Seasonality Type
text:
Using Visualization to Determine Seasonality Type
Many times, a simple line plot will be enough to determine whether our time series has additive or multiplicative seasonality.
We will use the flights data set from the seaborn package in Python as an example.

#Necessary imports
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

#Load flights data into 'flights' dataframe
flights = sns.load_dataset("flights")

#You will often need to convert your data into a more usable form, usually with some type of time index.
#This code converts the 'year' and 'month' columns into a single datatime column then sets that column as our index.

flights['date'] = pd.to_datetime(
    flights['year'].astype(str) + '-' + flights['month'].astype(str), format='%Y-%b'
)

flights = flights.set_index('date')

#Separate the target feature into a series. We no longer need the month/year columns since our index  already has that information.
y = flights['passengers']

#The easiest and quickest way to visualize the data is with the .plot method. This gives you a quick line graph.
y.plot(figsize=(8,6))
plt.title('Flight Passengers: 1949-1960')
plt.ylabel('Passengers (Thousands)')
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.show();








Now, look carefully at the seasonal fluctuations (the peaks and valleys) in this line graph.
Notice how the fluctuations get bigger as the trend increases over time.
This is a strong indicator of multiplicative seasonality.
If, on the other hand, the fluctuations stayed fairly consistent - even as the underlying trend increased - we would have evidence of additive seasonality.
What would happen if we assumed incorrectly that our data had additive seasonality?
Well, let’s use statsmodels seasonal_decompose function, with the model parameter set to “additive” instead of “multiplicative” and see what happens.

from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose

flights_decomp = seasonal_decompose(
                    y,
                    model='additive',
                    #model='multiplicative'
                )
fig = flights_decomp.plot()
fig.set_size_inches(8, 6);








Look carefully at the “Resid” plot (the 4th plot). This plot shows the remaining noise in the data once the trend and seasonal components have been accounted for. Notice how the residuals flare out at the ends, rather than staying consistent and tightly clustered around 0.
This should be a red flag. There is something in our decomposition that is not properly recognizing the underlying structure of the time series.
Let’s switch the model parameter to “multiplicative” and see whether our residual plot looks any better.

from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose

flights_decomp = seasonal_decompose(
                    y,
                    #model='additive',
                    model='multiplicative'
                )
fig = flights_decomp.plot()
fig.set_size_inches(8, 6);








Indeed, these residuals look much better. They are clustered closely to 1.0, which is what you would normally hope to see with multiplicative seasonality. There is no “flaring out” at the ends like we saw before either. This confirms what we expected from our line graph; our flights data set has multiplicative seasonality.

title: Additive vs. Multiplicative Seasonality
text:
Conclusion
In conclusion, once you recognize seasonal structure in your time series, you should try to identify whether your seasonality is additive or multiplicative.
This will impact future steps in your data analysis, processing, and model creation.

title: Differencing
text:
ARMA models require a stationary time series in order to work properly. If you are unfamiliar with the concept of stationarity, I encourage you to check out this article before moving forward.
If you determine that your time series is non-stationary - whether through visualization, statistical tests, or both - and you intend to build an auto-regression and/or moving average model (ARMA), you will need to make your data stationary. How can this be done? Through a simple process called differencing.
In this article we will explore what differencing is, how it can usually make a nonstationary time series stationary, and then walk through an easy way to perform differencing in Python.

title: Differencing
text:
What is Differencing?
Differencing, very simply, means calculating the change (i.e. the difference) between instances within your time series.
For example, if your time series was (0, 3, 2, 5, 5, 1, 7), then the differenced time series would be (3, -1, 3, 0, -4, 6), the difference between each “hop”. Think, “up 3”, “down 1”, “up 3”, “stay the same”, “down 4”, and “up 6”.
Differencing can be done at other intervals than just from each successive instance. Seasonal differencing is an example of this, where you calculate the difference between each successive seasonal instance. For example, you might calculate the difference between January 2025 and January 2026, February 2025 and February 2026, March 2025 and March 2026, etc. for monthly seasonal data.
In its simplest form though, differencing just implies taking the change between each successive instance. In essence, you are just converting your original time series of values into a time series of the change between values.

title: Differencing
text:
How does Differencing Work?
Interestingly, the change from instance to instance is often (though not always) relatively stable in mean and variance, even if the underlying time series is quite unstable.
Occasionally, you may need to difference your time series data more than once to achieve stationarity. If you find yourself differencing more than 2-3 times, however, you may need to consider other methods of working with your time series.

title: Differencing
text:
Conclusion
Differencing is a simple process that can generally be used to make a non-stationary time series stationary. We can difference our time series data using Pandas .diff() function. This is an important step in preparing your data for use in a statistical model like ARIMA.
The Google Stock Price data set used in this article was sourced from https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/varpit94/google-stock-data

title: Naive Forecasting Basics
text: In this article, we will explore the topic of naive forecasting models. We will explain the idea behind these simple models and what they are used for. Finally, we will walk through an example of building one in Python.

title: Naive Forecasting Basics
text:
What is a Naive Forecast?
The idea behind a naive forecast is very simple: the most recent value becomes the next forecasted value.
In terms of weather, a naive forecast would be like saying, “Today’s temperature was 42 degrees, so I expect tomorrow’s forecast will be 42 degrees.”
Sounds pretty simple, right? It is simple. That’s actually the beauty of naive forecasts. Surprisingly, for many time series, this forecasting method can work quite well. Where they often fall short is when your time series has seasonality or trend. However, naive forecasts can be expanded upon to account for those time series structures as well.
For now, though, we will stick with just our simple naive forecast with no seasonality or trend.

title: Naive Forecasting Basics
section: How can we use Naive Forecasts?
text:
How can we use Naive Forecasts?
Sometimes a naive forecast is used as a production model. These are cases when the best way to predict the future is with the most recent value in the past. They are easy to set up, not resource intensive, and very simple to explain.
However, where naive forecasts are most often used is as a benchmark or baseline forecasting model. They set the bar for every other model you build. When you are exploring types of forecasting models for your time series, make sure a naive model is one that you build and validate against. If a more advanced model cannot outperform the naive model, this should call into question whether the complexity of the advanced model adds any true value.

title: Naive Forecasting Basics
section: What are the limitations of Naive Forecasts?
text:
What are the limitations of Naive Forecasts?
Naive forecasts can be too simple for a time series that possesses structure. Another important limitation is that a naive forecast, in its simplest form, can only forecast a flat line as it extends into the future. This means a basic naive forecasting model’s predictive power can degrade very quickly.

title: Naive Forecasting Basics
section: How to Build a Naive Model in Python
text:
How to Build a Naive Model in Python
Building a simple naive model in Python is easy. You can use Pandas .shift() method to “slide” your data forward by one instance. This shifted series becomes your fitted values. Future forecasts will simply take on whatever the last value is in your training set.
More information about Pandas .shift() method is available here
Before we get started, let’s prepare our data. The following code uses the flights data set from Seaborn. For more info about this data set, visit the seaborn documentation located here

#Necessary imports
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

#Load flights data into 'flights' dataframe
flights = sns.load_dataset("flights")

#You will often need to convert your data into a more usable form, usually with some type of time index.
#This code converts the 'year' and 'month' columns into a single datetime column then sets that column as our index.

flights['date'] = pd.to_datetime(
    flights['year'].astype(str) + '-' + flights['month'].astype(str), format='%Y-%b'
)

flights = flights.set_index('date')

#Separate the target feature into a series. We no longer need the month/year columns since our index already has that information.
y = flights['passengers']


#We will split our data into train and test sets
y_train, y_test = train_test_split(y, shuffle=False, train_size=.8) #Notice, the "shuffle" parameter is set to false here. It defaults to true.

Now that our data is loaded, we are ready to move forward with getting our fitted values.
It is important to note, you will introduce missing values into your series for however many rows you shift with the .shift() method. You can drop these rows using Pandas dropna() method.

fitted_values = y_train.shift(1) #Shifting by 1 to get our simple naive fitted values
fitted_values = fitted_values.dropna() #Dropping the null value introduced by the shift

We have successfully generated our fitted values. Let’s now generate our forecast for the test set period. In this case, the final value of our training set will become the forecast for the entirety of the test set.

future_forecast_value = y_train.iloc[-1] #Grab the last value of our train set

forecasts = pd.Series(future_forecast_value, index=y_test.index) #Create a series with the same index as our test set that uses that one future value

forecasts.head(5)

date
1958-08-01    491
1958-09-01    491
1958-10-01    491
1958-11-01    491
1958-12-01    491
dtype: int64


As you can see, our naive forecast model produces a constant value of 491. Let’s use a visualization to get an idea for how well our naive forecast captures this time series.

#Combining fitted values and forecasts for simpler viewing
combined_fitted_and_forecasts = pd.concat([fitted_values, forecasts], axis=0)
combined_fitted_and_forecasts.name = 'forecasts'

#Combining with y for visualization purposes
combined_forecasts_actuals = pd.concat([y, combined_fitted_and_forecasts], axis=1).dropna()

combined_forecasts_actuals.plot(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.axvline(x=y_test.index[0], c='red', linestyle='--', label='Start of Test Set')
plt.title('Naive Forecast vs. Actuals - Flight Passengers')
plt.ylabel('Passengers (Thousands)')
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.legend()
plt.show();








The visualization drives the limitation of this model home. It does not do well at capturing the seasonality or trend in the flights time series once it enters the test period. For a data set without these structural components, however, a naive forecast may do quite well. Nevertheless, we have created what will serve as our most basic baseline forecast - one which future more advanced forecasting models will be compared to.

title: Naive Forecasting Basics
text:
Conclusion
In conclusion, naive forecasts are among the simplest time series models available. They are sometimes used for production forecasts, but more often they serve as baseline models to compare with more advanced model options. Creating a naive forecast is simple in Python. It could also be easily done in Microsoft Excel.
In future articles, we will explore how to add seasonality and trend to our naive model to make it more competitive.

title: Seasonal Naive Forecasting
text:
As described in our article on simple naive forecasting models, one of the major limitations of a simple naive forecasting model is that it cannot account for seasonality in time series data.
As a reminder, seasonal variations refer to recurring fluctuations that happen at consistent frequencies. For more information about seasonality and other time series structures, feel free to check our article on time series structures here.
In this article, we will walk through how you can build upon a simple naive forecast by accounting for seasonal variations in your time series data. This one step alone can often take what may seem like an overly simplistic model and turn it into a very competitive baseline to compare more advanced time series models against.

title: Seasonal Naive Forecasting
text:
The Basic Idea
If you understand how a simple naive forecast works, it is easy to grasp how a seasonal naive forecast works. You might recall that with a simple naive forecast, you are essentially just shifting your time series 1 step forward. In other words, what happens at t becomes the forecast for t+1. The most recent past value becomes the future projected value.
A seasonal naive forecasting model uses that same principle from a simple naive model - the past values become the forecast; however, rather than simply taking the most recent value (shifting 1 instance), we shift according to the seasonal duration. For monthly data with a yearly cycle, we shift by 12. For daily data with a weekly cycle, we shift by 7. For quarterly data with a yearly cycle, we shift by 4.
Let’s use yearly seasonality as an illustration. Imagine you are a data analyst for a large online toy retailer. You are attempting to forecast toy sales for December of this year - the peak month. A simple naive forecast would use November’s toy sales value (or whatever the most recent available value was) to predict December’s forecasted toy sales. A seasonal naive forecast, on the other hand, would use last December’s toy sales to predict next December’s toy sales. So, rather than shifting by 1, you’re shifting by 12. The same concept would extend to other forms of seasonality (weekly, quarterly, etc.).

title: Seasonal Naive Forecasting
text:
A Python Example
Having discussed the general concept behind a seasonal naive forecast, let’s walk through a simple implementation in Python. We will use pandas’ .shift() method again. This time, however, we will shift by the seasonal period, rather than just shifting by 1 instance. More information about pandas’ .shift() method is available here.
For this example, we will be using a dataset that tracks monthly average US temperatures (in degrees Fahrenheit) from 1975 to 2025. This data was retrieved from the NCEI Climate at a Glance National Time Series site here.

#Necessary imports
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

#Load US average temp data from 1975-2025

data = pd.read_csv('us_temps_1975-2025.csv')

#Prepare datetime index

data['date'] = pd.to_datetime(data['date'].astype(str), format='%Y%m')
data = data.set_index('date').asfreq('MS') #Set index and ensure frequency is specified as month start

data.head(5) #Check the first five rows

Let’s take a moment to visualize our data. In a real-world project, you would go a lot deeper in the exploration stage, but for our purposes we will just use a simple line graph and a basic time series decomposition using statsmodels’ seasonal_decompose function.

#Build a basic line plot of the data

data.plot(figsize=(8, 6), legend=False)
plt.title('US Monthly Average Temperatures: 1975-2025')
plt.ylabel('Temperature (Degrees Fahrenheit)')
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.show();








The fluctuations appear to be seasonal, and there does not appear to be a strong trend present from the raw line plot. Let’s proceed with decomposing our time series.

decomp = seasonal_decompose(
    data,
    model='additive' #Additive seasonality as we do not have evidence of multiplicative variation
)

fig = decomp.plot()
fig.set_size_inches(8, 6)








Our time series does appear to have a slight upward trend (2nd plot). In other words, recorded US average temperatures increased slightly from 1975 to 2025. For the purposes of this exercise, though, we will ignore that trend structure for now.
The seasonal component (3rd plot) very clearly shows what appears to be strong yearly (12-month) seasonality. This makes intuitive sense as temperatures are highest in summer months and lowest in winter months in the United States.
For our purposes, we have strong evidence that a seasonal naive forecast model may be appropriate for this time series. Let’s set apart a portion of our data as a test set using sklearn’s train_test_split function, being sure the shuffle parameter is set to False. We will reserve 24 months of data for testing purposes.

train, test = train_test_split(data, shuffle=False, test_size=24) #Shuffle set to False since we're working with a time series


#Quick gut check of the train and test set sizes
print("Train Set Size:", train.shape[0])
print("Test Set Size:", test.shape[0])

Train Set Size: 588
Test Set Size: 24


Okay, now for the fun part. Let’s first generate our fitted values for our training set. We will use .dropna() to drop the null values that result from this shift.

#Generate fitted values by shifting the data
fitted_values = train.shift(12).dropna()

fitted_values.head()

Now, let’s take the last 12 values of our training set and use them as our forecast for the test set period.

forecast_values = train['temp'].iloc[-12:] #Extract last seasonal period

forecast_values = pd.concat([forecast_values, forecast_values], ignore_index=True) #Repeat the seasonal period twice to match length of test set (24 months)
#Note, there are more flexible ways to do this in situations when the test set size is not a multiple of the seasonal period
#This method works for the purpose of our illustration here

forecast_values.index = test.index #Change index to match the test set index

We have forecasted for the duration of our test set. Now let’s use visualization to see how well our seasonal naive forecast performed on the test set. Note that we will limit the view to start at 2010 to make it easier to see the seasonal fluctuations and alignment.

#Combine fitted values and forecasted values into one dataframe
combined_fitted_forecasts = pd.concat([fitted_values, forecast_values], axis=0)

# Add the actual values into the same dataframe for easy visualization
combined_actual_forecasts = pd.concat([data, combined_fitted_forecasts], axis=1).dropna() #Dropping null values for which there is no forecast

#Rename columns
combined_actual_forecasts.columns = ['Actuals', 'Forecasts']

#Plot the results
combined_actual_forecasts['2010-01-01':].plot(figsize=(8, 6), legend=True)
plt.axvline(x=test.index[0], c='red', linestyle='--', label='Start of Test Set')
plt.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1.0), loc="upper left")
plt.title('US Monthly Average Temps: Forecast vs. Actuals')
plt.ylabel('Temperature (Degrees Fahrenheit)')
plt.xlabel('Date')
plt.show();








Based on this visualization alone, we can surmise that our seasonal naive forecasting model does a decent job of capturing the overall structure of the US average temperature data. Both the fitted values and the test-period forecast values show the correct seasonal variation. This suggests that one year’s average temperatures each month are a good indication of the next year’s average temperatures.
In a real-world project, we would now want to compare other types of models such as Exponential Smoothing with Seasonality or SARIMA and use metrics like RMSE or MAE to determine which model is most appropriate. For now though, we have demonstrated that seasonal naive can be a strong baseline forecasting model for time series that have seasonality but little to no trend.

title: Seasonal Naive Forecasting
text:
Conclusion
To sum up, a simple naive model is often too simplistic, especially for time series that have seasonal fluctuations. We can easily adjust our approach in Python to account for seasonality in our data. This provides us with a better forecasting model to which more advanced models can be compared. Sometimes, a simple model like seasonal naive can outperform even more sophisticated time series forecasting models. This forecasting model should be one every data professional has in their tool belt.

title: Train-Test Split for Time Series
text:
One of the most important steps when building machine learning models is splitting your data into training and testing sets.
The training data is what you use to build, fit, and choose your models; the testing data is used at the end of the process to see how your chosen model would perform on unseen data. This helps you to approximate how the model would do “in the real world”.
Time series modeling also requires train-test splits. There are more advanced ways of checking your time series models such as rolling horizon cross-validation which we will cover in future articles. Even if you use cross-validation, however, most of the time, you will still want to do a train-test split so you have a part of your data that is reserved for testing at the end of your project.
In this article, we will look at an important difference when splitting time series data. We will also walk through a basic example in Python.

title: Train-Test Split for Time Series
text:
One of the most important steps when building machine learning models is splitting your data into training and testing sets.
The training data is what you use to build, fit, and choose your models; the testing data is used at the end of the process to see how your chosen model would perform on unseen data. This helps you to approximate how the model would do “in the real world”.
Time series modeling also requires train-test splits. There are more advanced ways of checking your time series models such as rolling horizon cross-validation which we will cover in future articles. Even if you use cross-validation, however, most of the time, you will still want to do a train-test split so you have a part of your data that is reserved for testing at the end of your project.
In this article, we will look at an important difference when splitting time series data. We will also walk through a basic example in Python.

title: Train-Test Split for Time Series
section: Problems with Shuffling Time Series Data
text:
Problems with Shuffling Time Series Data
With non-time series data sets (cross-sectional data), you often will shuffle your data as part of the train-test split process. This helps to ensure that the training and testing set both have a good, randomized mix of instances.
However, shuffling time series data is almost always a big mistake.
Time series data, unlike cross-sectional data, often possesses autocorrelation and structures like trend, seasonality, or cycles. These aspects of the data are often critical in understanding and modeling your time series. Shuffling the data will destroy this underlying autocorrelation and structure. This will severely hinder your modeling of the data or forecasts later on.
If you shuffle time series data, it can cause a type of data leakage specific to time series. In this case, it can move instances that are later in time ahead of instances that occurred earlier in time. This could lead to you training on future data and testing on past data. In other words, future data could be used to predict past data. This is not realistic for real-world modeling.
Remember, with time series, order matters.

title: Train-Test Split for Time Series
text:
Train-Test Split in Python
In the following code cells, we will walk through a simple example of a train-test split in Python.
We will use sklearn’s train_test_split function to achieve this. For more information about this function, visit sklearn’s official documentation here.
First, we will import the necessary libraries.

#Necessary imports
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split #This is the train-test split function we will use

Next, we will load the flights data set from seaborn. For more info about this data set, visit this seaborn documentation. We will also set up the time index.

#Load flights data into 'flights' dataframe
flights = sns.load_dataset("flights")

#You will often need to convert your data into a more usable form, usually with some type of time index.

#This code converts the 'year' and 'month' columns into a single datetime column then sets that column as our index.

flights['date'] = pd.to_datetime(
    flights['year'].astype(str) + '-' + flights['month'].astype(str), format='%Y-%b'
)

flights = flights.set_index('date')

#Separate the target feature into a series. We no longer need the month/year columns since our index already has that information.
y = flights['passengers']

Now, we have our “y”, which is the full time series data we will work with. We are ready to split it into train and test sets.
By default, sklearn’s train_test_split function shuffles your data. This is what we want to avoid, so we will set the shuffle parameter to False to override the default behavior.
We will set our training set size to use 80% of our data. The remaining 20% will be reserved as a test set.

y_train, y_test = train_test_split(y, shuffle=False, train_size=.8) #Notice, the "shuffle" parameter is set to False here. It defaults to true.

#Let's check the size of our train and test sets as a gut check. 
print('Train Set Size:', len(y_train), 'rows')
print('Test Set Size:', len(y_test), 'rows')

Train Set Size: 115 rows
Test Set Size: 29 rows


We can confirm that the start and end dates of our train and test set are still in chronological order.

print('Train Start:', y_train.index[0])
print('Train End:', y_train.index[-1])
print('Test Start:', y_test.index[0])
print('Test End:', y_test.index[-1])

Train Start: 1949-01-01 00:00:00
Train End: 1958-07-01 00:00:00
Test Start: 1958-08-01 00:00:00
Test End: 1960-12-01 00:00:00


Success! We now have divided our time series data into training and testing sets while respecting the sequential order of our data. In a real project, we would use y_train to build our time series models, and reserve the y_test to check our final model selection on unseen data.
